title: Copilot for Pull Requests & Code Review

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Code review is one of the highest-leverage activities in a software team — it catches bugs, improves quality, spreads knowledge, and enforces standards. It's also slow, inconsistent, and often blocked on reviewer availability.

GitHub Copilot participates in your code review process directly on GitHub.com:
- **Auto-generating PR descriptions** so reviewers understand changes immediately
- **Acting as a reviewer** — reviewing your PR for bugs, security issues, and style before human reviewers see it
- **Suggesting specific fixes** that can be applied in one click
- **Implementing its own suggestions** by raising a child PR with the fixes already made
- **Automatic review** on every push — catching issues the moment code is pushed

This lesson teaches you to use all of these capabilities so your PRs are cleaner, faster, and more complete before any human touches them.

## Generating PR Descriptions with Copilot

Vague PR descriptions are a constant problem — they waste reviewer time, make code archaeology harder, and cause bugs to slip through because reviewers don't know what to focus on.

Copilot can generate a complete, accurate PR description from the diff alone.

### How to Generate a PR Description

**Method 1 — On GitHub.com (PR editor)**
1. Create or open a PR
2. In the description editor, click the **Copilot icon** (sparkle) in the toolbar
3. Select **Generate summary**
Copilot reads the full diff and generates a description covering: what changed, why it changed (if derivable from the code), and what reviewers should focus on.

**Method 2 — In Copilot CLI:**
```
/diff
```
Then ask:
```
Write a pull request description for these changes. Include: a 3-bullet summary, 
technical approach, testing coverage, and risk level.
```

**Method 3 — In VS Code Chat:**
With your branch checked out:
```
@workspace Write a PR description for the changes on this branch vs main. 
Use this format: Summary (3 bullets), Technical details (2-3 sentences), 
Testing done, Risk (Low/Medium/High with reason).
```

### What Makes a Good Copilot PR Description?

Copilot reads the code diff to infer intent. It works best when:
- Commit messages are meaningful ("fix: validate email before DB insert" tells it a lot)
- Code changes are atomic — one PR, one purpose
- The diff is clean (no stray whitespace changes, no unrelated files)

Always review the generated description. Copilot can infer what changed but may not know *why* — add the business context it can't see from the code alone.

## Requesting a Copilot Code Review

Copilot can act as a reviewer on any pull request — running the same kind of review a senior developer would: checking for bugs, security issues, logic errors, and missing tests.

### Manual Review Request

1. Open a PR on GitHub.com
2. In the right sidebar, under **Reviewers**, click the gear icon
3. Type **Copilot** in the search box
4. Select **Copilot** to request a review
5. Wait — the review usually takes under 30 seconds

Scroll down to see Copilot's review comments. Each comment is on a specific line with:
- The concern identified
- Why it's a problem
- A suggested fix (often as a one-click code block you can apply)

### Automatic Review (All PRs)

You can configure Copilot to automatically review every PR without a manual request:

1. Go to your GitHub profile → **Copilot settings**
2. Find **Automatic Copilot code review**
3. Set to **Enabled**
4. Optionally enable **Review new pushes** — Copilot re-reviews every time you push a new commit
5. Optionally enable **Review draft pull requests** — catch issues even earlier

With automatic review enabled, Copilot's review appears within seconds of PR creation — before any human reviewer has opened the PR.

### Review Effort Levels

Copilot supports two effort levels for reviews:

| Level | Speed | Depth | Best for |
|-------|-------|-------|----------|
| **Low** (default) | Fast | Standard — bugs, security, style | Routine changes |
| **Medium** | Slower | Deep reasoning model — complex logic, cross-service security | Security-sensitive code, complex features |

To use Medium effort, request the review via the GitHub REST API or in your team's branch protection rules. Medium reviews consume more AI credits and GitHub Actions minutes.

## Applying and Implementing Suggestions

Copilot's review comments include actionable suggestions — not just observations.

### One-Click Application

For simple fixes (renaming a variable, adding a null check, fixing a typo), Copilot's suggestion appears as a code block with an **Apply suggestion** button. Clicking it updates the file directly and creates a commit. No manual editing needed.

You can also batch multiple suggestions: tick the checkbox on each suggestion you want to apply, then click **Commit suggestions** to apply all selected ones in a single commit.

### Implement Suggestion (Multi-Step Fixes)

For more complex changes, Copilot offers an **Implement suggestion** button on a review comment. This does something more powerful: it creates a **child pull request** — a new PR targeting your branch — where the Copilot cloud agent has already implemented the fix. You review the child PR, and if it looks good, merge it into your branch. Your original PR then includes the fix.

This is the workflow for:
- Fixes that require changes across multiple files
- Refactors suggested by a reviewer that would take 30+ minutes manually
- Security patches that need careful, correct implementation

### Copilot Cloud Agent on Issues

For even earlier intervention: on any GitHub Issue, click **Assign to Copilot**. The cloud agent:
1. Reads the issue
2. Explores the relevant parts of the codebase
3. Creates an implementation plan
4. Writes the code on a new branch
5. Opens a PR for your review

You review and merge, or request changes. This takes work items from issue to PR with no manual implementation for well-defined tasks.

**Billing note (from June 2026):** Each Copilot code review is billed as AI Credits under the usage-based billing model. On private repositories, reviews also consume GitHub Actions minutes. Monitor your organization's usage in GitHub organization settings → Usage → Copilot. For teams doing many PRs daily, Medium effort reviews add up — use Low effort as the default and reserve Medium for high-risk changes.

## Customizing Reviews with Instruction Files

Copilot's code review can be customized to focus on things that matter to your team specifically — not just generic best practices.

### Adding Review Instructions

Copilot's code review uses the same `copilot-instructions.md` and path-specific instruction files covered in lesson 6-13. But you can also add review-specific instructions.

Copilot reads instructions from the **base branch** of the PR. So your instructions in `main` apply to all PRs merging into main.

### Review-Specific Instructions Example

Add a section to `.github/copilot-instructions.md`:

```markdown
## Code Review Guidelines

When reviewing code, prioritize these concerns in order:
1. Security: Any code that accesses user data, handles authentication, or makes external calls
2. Data validation: All inputs from external sources must be validated before use
3. Audit logging: Any function that creates, modifies, or deletes records must log the action
4. Error handling: Errors must be caught and logged — never silently discarded
5. Test coverage: New public functions should have at least one test

Do NOT comment on:
- Formatting or whitespace (handled by our linter)
- Minor naming style issues
- Comments explaining obvious code

For government/compliance code: always flag any output that might expose PII, even if it's behind a permission check.
```

### Path-Specific Review Rules

Create `.github/instructions/review-security.instructions.md`:
```markdown
---
applyTo: "**/auth/**"
---

For authentication code specifically:
- Verify that session tokens are not logged
- Check that failed auth attempts are rate-limited
- Ensure sensitive operations re-verify identity rather than relying on session state
- Flag any use of MD5 or SHA1 for password hashing
```

Copilot applies these extra rules only when reviewing files in the auth directory.

sections.title: Your First Copilot-Reviewed PR
sections.content:
Create a real pull request and use Copilot as your first reviewer.

**Step 1 — Make a real change** in a project that's hosted on GitHub. Any meaningful change: a bug fix, a small feature, a refactor. Make at least 5-10 lines of real code changes.

**Step 2 — Generate a PR description**
Before creating the PR, use one of the description methods from this lesson:
- In VS Code chat: `@workspace Write a PR description for the changes on this branch`
- Or use the Copilot icon in the GitHub PR editor after creating the PR

**Step 3 — Create the PR** on GitHub.com. Paste the generated description. Add any context Copilot couldn't infer (business reason, stakeholder context).

**Step 4 — Request a Copilot review**
In the Reviewers section, add Copilot. Wait for the review.

**Step 5 — Evaluate each review comment:**
- Is the issue identified genuine?
- Is the suggested fix correct?
- Apply suggestions you agree with using the one-click button
- For suggestions you disagree with, reply explaining why

**Step 6 — Make at least 2 fixes** based on Copilot's review. These should be real issues, not superficial changes.

**Outcome:** A PR that's been pre-screened by AI before any human reviewer sees it. How many issues did Copilot find that you missed?

sections.title: Workshop A — Customize Review Instructions
sections.content:
Write review instructions that make Copilot focus on what matters in your specific context.

**Step 1 — Audit what Copilot focused on** in the main workshop review. List its top 3-4 concerns.

**Step 2 — Evaluate relevance.** Were these the right things to focus on for your project? Or were there:
- Important issues it missed?
- Irrelevant concerns it flagged?
- Domain-specific rules it didn't know about?

**Step 3 — Write review instructions** in your `.github/copilot-instructions.md`:
- Add a section specifically about what to prioritize in reviews
- Add what NOT to comment on (things your linter or formatter handles)
- Add any project-specific rules that are non-obvious

For government/regulated projects, add:
```markdown
## Code Review — Priority Rules

Always check for:
- Any variable or log statement that might contain: employee IDs, tax numbers, 
  health data, or financial account details
- Functions that write to the database without a corresponding audit log
- Error messages that might reveal system architecture to end users
```

**Step 4 — Create a new PR** (or modify an existing one) and request another Copilot review.

**Step 5 — Compare** to the first review. Does Copilot now focus on the right things? Iterate the instructions until the review output matches what you actually want to catch.

sections.title: Workshop B — Implement Suggestion Workflow
sections.content:
Practice the full Implement Suggestion workflow — from review comment to merged fix.

**Setup:** You need a PR on GitHub.com with at least one Copilot review comment that suggests a non-trivial fix (not just a one-liner).

**Step 1 — Find a complex review suggestion.** Look for a Copilot comment that suggests something multi-step — add error handling, refactor a function, add input validation across multiple places.

**Step 2 — Click Implement suggestion** on that comment. If the button isn't available, look for **Open in Copilot** or request via the comment: type `@copilot Please implement this suggestion`.

**Step 3 — Watch the cloud agent work.** Copilot creates a new branch and PR. It may take 1-3 minutes.

**Step 4 — Review the child PR.** This is where your judgment is critical:
- Did the cloud agent correctly interpret the suggestion?
- Did it introduce any new issues?
- Does the fix handle edge cases?
- Does it match your code style?

**Step 5 — Merge or request changes** on the child PR. If merged, verify your original PR now includes the fix.

**The key skill here:** Reviewing what an AI agent implemented on your behalf. This is different from reviewing AI suggestions — the agent has written complete code that you must evaluate as carefully as any human-authored PR.

sections.title: Workshop C — Issue-to-PR with Copilot Cloud Agent
sections.content:
Use the Copilot cloud agent to take a well-defined issue all the way to a draft PR.

**Step 1 — Write a high-quality issue** on one of your GitHub repositories. The issue must be:
- Specific (not 'improve the code')
- Self-contained (all information needed is in the issue)
- Well-defined (a developer reading it knows exactly what done looks like)

Example of a good issue:
```
Add input validation to the /api/users POST endpoint

Currently the endpoint accepts any JSON body. It should validate:
- email: required, valid email format
- name: required, string, 2-100 characters
- role: required, must be one of: ['viewer', 'editor', 'admin']

Return 400 with a JSON error listing which fields failed and why.
Test file: tests/test_users.py — add tests for valid input and each validation failure case.
```

**Step 2 — Assign the issue to Copilot.**
In the issue's right sidebar → Assignees → search for and select **Copilot**.

**Step 3 — Watch the agent work.** It explores the repo, creates an implementation plan, and opens a PR. You'll get a notification when it's ready (usually 3-10 minutes).

**Step 4 — Review the PR thoroughly.** The agent is autonomous — it may interpret the issue differently than intended, or make decisions about implementation style that differ from yours.

**Step 5 — Request changes or merge.** Treat this exactly as you'd treat a junior developer's PR — thorough review, specific feedback, clear expectations.

**What to note:** For what kind of issues did the cloud agent do a great job? For what kind did it struggle? Write this down — it defines what you should and shouldn't assign to the cloud agent.

sections.title: Workshop D — Build a PR Review Workflow for Your Team
sections.content:
Design and document a standard PR workflow that integrates Copilot review into your team's process.

**Create a `PR-WORKFLOW.md`** in your repository's `.github/` folder.

**Section 1 — Author Checklist (before requesting review):**
- [ ] Generated PR description with Copilot and verified accuracy
- [ ] Added context Copilot can't infer: business reason, stakeholder impact
- [ ] Requested Copilot review as first reviewer
- [ ] Addressed all High and Medium severity Copilot comments
- [ ] Applied auto-fixable suggestions with one click
- [ ] Tests pass

**Section 2 — Review Effort Guideline:**
Define when your team uses Low vs Medium effort Copilot review:
- Low: routine changes, bug fixes, test additions, documentation
- Medium: authentication code, database schema changes, external API integrations, security-related changes

**Section 3 — How to Respond to Copilot Comments:**
- Agree: apply the suggestion (one click)
- Disagree: reply with your reasoning (Copilot's review is a Comment, not a blocking review)
- Unclear: ask Copilot for clarification in a reply

**Section 4 — When to Use Cloud Agent Implementation:**
List 3-4 types of Copilot suggestions that are best implemented by the cloud agent (complex refactors, multi-file changes) vs. implemented manually.

**Section 5 — Government/Compliance Addendum:**
Any code changes in [list sensitive areas] require Medium effort review AND human review by [designated role] before merge.

**Outcome:** A documented team workflow that makes AI code review a consistent, reliable part of how your team ships code.

sections.question: Copilot reviews your PR and leaves a comment saying 'This function doesn't validate the input before processing it.' The comment has an 'Apply suggestion' button. You click it. What happens?
options: Copilot opens a chat session where you discuss the validation approach
The suggested code change is applied to the file and committed directly to your PR branch
A draft comment is created that you must edit and manually commit
The cloud agent creates a child PR with the validation added
sections.explanation: The 'Apply suggestion' button in GitHub's PR interface directly commits the suggested code change to your PR branch. It's equivalent to editing the file yourself and pushing — but in one click. The commit message is auto-generated noting it's applying a Copilot suggestion. If you want to batch multiple suggestions into one commit, tick the checkboxes on each and use 'Commit suggestions'. For complex multi-file changes, 'Implement suggestion' (different button) uses the cloud agent instead.

sections.question: You want Copilot to review every PR automatically without someone manually requesting it. What is the correct way to set this up?
options: Add Copilot as a required reviewer in your branch protection rules
In GitHub profile → Copilot settings → enable Automatic Copilot code review
Edit the repository's CODEOWNERS file to route all files to Copilot
Create a GitHub Actions workflow that requests a Copilot review on every PR open event
sections.explanation: Automatic Copilot code review is a setting in your personal Copilot settings (or organization Copilot settings for org-wide setup). Enable it and Copilot automatically reviews every new PR without manual requests. You can also enable 'Review new pushes' so Copilot re-reviews after each new commit. Note: Copilot's review is always a Comment, never an Approve or Request Changes — so it doesn't count toward required approvals and won't block merging.

sections.content: **Lesson 6-15 complete.** Copilot's PR capabilities — description generation, automated review, one-click fix application, and cloud agent implementation — can make your PRs significantly cleaner and faster without adding reviewer burden. The key discipline: treat Copilot's review as a first pass that catches obvious issues, not a replacement for human review of logic, intent, and business context. Lesson 6-16 covers Copilot Extensions and the Skills Marketplace — adding specialized capabilities beyond the built-in tools.
